People said the North Slope was over, the big discoveries had been made, the basin was in decline. People were wrong. 

There is nothing inherently wise about a crowd. No one ever built the future by following the herd. Bill Armstrong saw what so many others missed, believed in himself and his team, sold his vision to Santos (Oil Search) and Repsol, and today with their execution and commitment we celebrate the start of the long hoped for North Slope Renaissance.

There’s an important lesson in this milestone. Our best days can be ahead, but only if we have the courage and conviction to do what some may say can’t be done. If we choose a timid path we will be guaranteed to live in someone else’s future; but if we are bold, we have the opportunity to build an incredible and prosperous future of our own choosing.

Illegal drugs like fentanyl have destroyed the lives of young people and families across our state. That’s why I fought to close the border to illegal migrants and pass the Halt Fentanyl Act, making sure penalties for trafficking were increased and copycat substances were made illegal. Alaska’s next generation deserves the chance to grow up in safe communities.

Fentanyl has devastated so many Alaskan families. When I ran for Congress, I made a promise to work to take this challenge head on. That’s why I’m proud to have co-sponsored and passed into law the HALT Fentanyl Act, a bill that increases mandatory minimum sentences to 10 years for dealers and permanently classifies Fentanyl and its analogues as Schedule I substances, closing an open loophole in the law.

Cracking down on crime and enforcing border security saves innocent lives, and saves friends and families the pain of immeasurable loss.

But let us be clear-eyed and honest about what reparations truly mean in American history and in the soul of our Republic.

From the earliest days under our Constitution, reparations were never about mere cash payouts or ongoing entitlements. They were solemn acts to right grave wrongs, restore dignity, and preserve peace among civilized nations and within our own borders—without compromising the sacred freedoms that define us.

Recall President Thomas Jefferson in 1807: When the British warship HMS Leopard brazenly attacked the USS Chesapeake off Virginia's coast, killing and wounding American sailors and impressing our citizens, the outrage was universal. War loomed. Yet Jefferson, ever the statesman, chose a path of principled restraint. He demanded Britain disavow the act and provide reparations—financial compensation—to the United States. Not to buy silence, but to affirm justice and avert bloodshed. This was diplomacy rooted in honor, not appeasement.

In more recent times, we have seen reparations used precisely to confront our own failures:

In 1946, Congress created the Indian Claims Commission to address treaty violations and land seizures from Native American tribes—seeking to make amends for broken promises etched into our nation's soil.

In 1971, President Nixon signed the Alaska Native Claims Settlement Act, transferring vast lands and funds to resolve aboriginal claims, honoring indigenous rights.

Finally, in 1988, the Civil Liberties Act provided $20,000 and a formal apology to each surviving Japanese American interned during World War II—acknowledging a shameful violation of civil liberties driven by fear and prejudice.

These were not handouts. They were acknowledgments of injustice, efforts to heal wounds, and commitments to do better—always in service to liberty, not in substitution for it.

Now consider the deepest wound in our history: chattel slavery, which denied millions their God-given free will, treated human beings as property, and trampled the very conscience and dignity protected by our First Amendment.

The true reparations due to those enslaved—and to their descendants—was freedom itself. The Emancipation Proclamation and the 13th Amendment declared: No more masters. No more chains. Slavery's legacy was ended at an unimaginable cost—over 600,000 lives lost in the Civil War, families shattered, a nation torn asunder—all to reaffirm that this is a land where no person owns another, where government exists to secure the blessings of liberty, not to dispense favors in lieu of it.

That sacrifice can never be fully repaid with dollars. The only fitting reparations—the only ones worthy of our heroes in blue and gray—are a government that never ceases recommitting to freedom for all. Justice for every American. The unyielding defense of liberty so that every citizen—Black, White, of every faith and background—can thrive without shackles, whether of iron or of dependency.

Do not let well-intentioned policies become chains on the conscience. Do not trade the priceless gift of freedom for fleeting benefits. True justice demands we recommit, together, to the arduous, eternal work of preserving liberty for ourselves and our posterity.

The Second Amendment is the only Amendment that represents a shared interest and liberty between the government and the people. It is a shared interest because it is derived directly from individual liberty.

James Madison originally placed the Second Amendment in Article I, Section 9 — between Clauses 3 and 4 — as one of the limits on Congress, since the Constitution had not yet been amended. Article I, Section 9 enumerates specific restrictions on legislative power.

The Militia was viewed as vital to our form of government and way of life because the public and general liberties secured by the states and the federal government are derived from our individual right to defend Life, Liberty, and the Pursuit of Happiness. The Second Amendment represents a solemn partnership: it not only declares our rights, but obligates the government to partner with the people to guard and secure them — using force when necessary — for the sole purpose of securing the Blessings of Liberty to ourselves, our families, and our way of life.

The Second Amendment protects both a collective and an individual right. It is the only right in the Constitution where the People and the Government are true partners in preserving and defending our way of life. The Constitution is not merely a list of enumerated powers; it is also a list of obligations placed upon government, and it directs government into this partnership.

Madison once stated that the Bill of Rights would be nothing but “parchment barriers.” This is true for every other right — except the Second Amendment. It adds force to the declaration and bridges the divide between individual, public, and general liberty, ensuring that our way of life both preserves and secures freedom.

“A well regulated Militia, being necessary to the security of a free State” is what the Supreme Court calls the prefatory clause. When the Second Amendment was moved from Article I, Section 9 and added to the end of the Constitution, it pointed back to Article I, Section 8, Clauses 15 and 16, which require the Militia to be well-regulated. The term “well-regulated Militia” refers to the elite citizen-soldiers, or Minutemen. The prefatory clause reminds government that the Second Amendment does not relieve it of its obligation to oversee every aspect of the Militia according to its enumerated powers. The operative clause — “the right of the people to keep and bear Arms, shall not be infringed” — tells government that this obligation does not extend to disarming the people themselves. The Arms of the people remain outside the scope of government’s regulatory power.

I am honored to have the endorsement of the CRPA. By Larry Thompson

We walk and drive past homeless people every day. Mostly, we do nothing.

Occasionally, stopped at a red light, we see a man approaching our car with a tattered cardboard sign asking for money to buy food. His proximity makes us nervous. His circumstances make us feel guilty.

First, government would provide matching funds, coordination, and oversight. Participating agencies would help identify housing, coordinate services, establish financial controls, and maintain a public record of spending and results.

Second, participating religious institutions would match government financing dollar for dollar by “passing the basket” during services through designated, voluntary Good Sam collections. Every government dollar awarded to a participating institution would require a dollar raised for the program. Participation would be voluntary for institutions and individual donors. Congregations could pool their collections through a shared Good Sam fund, allowing smaller institutions to participate together. Government payments would follow verification of the required private match. This would give congregations a concrete responsibility: help finance the work, help carry it out, and help account for its results.

Third, religious and community partners would organize practical support: meals, transportation, apartment furnishings, identification documents, employment assistance, and regular personal contact. Each organization would accept specific assignments within its capabilities.

Fourth, qualified professionals would provide case management, mental health care, and addiction treatment. Each person enrolled would have an assigned case manager and an individual plan for housing, care, and greater stability. Volunteers would receive training and support. They would strengthen professional services, with clear boundaries and someone responsible for following through.

Fifth, the public would see the results. Reports would track dollars spent, verified matching contributions, housing placements, housing retention, and connections to needed care. Independent audits would examine spending. Ineffective providers would face corrective action or replacement, while participants’ care continued.

The partnership would serve people regardless of faith. Nobody would have to pray, attend worship, or accept religious instruction to receive assistance. Public dollars and matching contributions would support authorized homeless services, with separate accounting from religious activities.

To those whose first response is to complain about “Church and State” before considering the people we could help, I would answer, " This is a proposed, simple, local, and temporary partnership to help mitigate or solve one human dilemma.  It's not attempting to set new government precedent.   

Serious questions deserve serious answers. Good Sam would have written safeguards, voluntary participation, equal access, and transparent finances. We can respect religious freedom while welcoming religious institutions willing to help their neighbors.

The five-year commitment would allow time to build partnerships and measure whether people remain housed. Annual reviews would guide improvements. At five years, the program would expire unless renewed after an independent evaluation and public review.

The goal would be fewer people returning to homelessness year after year.

Safe sidewalks, accessible businesses, and usable parks matter. So does the human being sleeping outside them. Moving someone to another block accomplishes little without a path toward stability.

No honest person can guarantee that one program will end every instance of homelessness. We can demand a plan that connects money, personal responsibility, qualified care, and lasting housing.

We can also stop treating compassion as something we outsource entirely to government.

Pass the basket. Recruit the volunteers. Assign the case managers. Open the books. Measure the results.

The next light will turn green. We will have somewhere to go.

Let us help our homeless neighbors find somewhere to go, too.

Where are the Good Samaritans?

Let the answer begin with us.

Illinois 14th Congressional District — Veterans for America First (VFAF), the original 2015 Veterans for Trump grassroots organization, proudly announces its endorsement of Jim Marter for Congress in Illinois’ 14th District for the 2026 election cycle.

Jim Marter is a proven conservative leader, grassroots organizer, and successful business owner with a long-standing record of public service and Republican Party leadership in Illinois. His work has supported industries including defense and aerospace, agriculture sciences, automotive, life sciences, energy, and manufacturing.

Raised in Bartonville, Illinois, Marter developed leadership skills early through academics and athletics, including NCAA Division I swimming at Purdue University. His commitment to faith, family, and community remains central to his life. He and his wife Jill have been married for 40 years, have four children and six grandchildren, and are active parishioners at St. Anne Parish in Oswego.

As a fisherman at heart, he understands the economic and cultural importance of Massachusetts’ fisheries, which have sustained generations. Tyler’s time on the Mattapoisett Select Board has honed his ability to listen to constituents, navigate complex local issues, and deliver practical solutions—skills he pledges to bring to Congress.

Tyler’s professional background is as diverse as the district he seeks to represent. His master’s in business equips him with a keen understanding of economic policy, budgeting, and fiscal management, which he believes are critical to addressing the nation’s ballooning deficits and economic uncertainty. He is a tireless advocate for the region’s fishermen, fighting to ensure their livelihoods are protected through policies that balance environmental stewardship with economic opportunity. Tyler is equally passionate about supporting veterans, recognizing their sacrifices and pushing for robust services and opportunities to help them thrive. His vision for CD9 is one of resilient communities, where practical, results-driven policies foster economic growth, preserve local traditions, and restore trust in government.

Tyler MacAllister’s campaign is built on a promise: to represent the heart and soul of Massachusetts’ South Coast, Cape, Islands, and South Shore with integrity, determination, and a relentless focus on results. 11 Sept 26 - TONIGHT WAS SPECIAL.    September 11 is always a solemn day for me. Twenty-five years later, we still remember the nearly 3,000 Americans who were taken from us, the first responders who ran toward danger, and the incredible unity and service that followed that terrible day. We must Never Forget. But tonight also reminded me of something important: community matters.  I had the pleasure of attending my friend Councilman Nathan Volke’s 8th Annual Crab Feast at Kurtz Beach—and what a night it was!  Nathan is a favorite son of Kurtz Beach and the surrounding community, and judging by the crowd, his crab feast has become one of the great annual gatherings in Maryland’s 3rd Congressional District.   Hundreds of people. Great food. Great conversations. Beautiful views right on the water. And a whole lot of Maryland crabs!    And yes… I ate too much. Again. 😂

Medicare for All. You’ve probably heard that phrase thrown around a lot over the last few months. My opponent has vied for this single payer “solution” to our health care system, but he accidentally slipped and said the quiet part out loud, "Medicare for All is not possible".  Our current healthcare system is broken and certainly needs to be fixed.  I think we can all agree on that.  

But while I can agree with my opponent that the current system needs fixing, there are so many issues with Medicare for All that he was actually fact checked by local media.  What they found is the very reason I disagree with his proposal:

1.  He's using outdated figures to push his ideology by saying M4A will save families $3,000 annually. 
FALSE: The AMA has never published any such study (links in comments).

2.  He references other studies that also claim monetary savings and a decrease in patient lives lost.
Both have been debunked or discredited (links in comments).

3.  While free health care for everyone sounds great, the price tag does not. The Congressional Budget Office puts the cost of Medicare for All at $1.5-$3 trillion per year (almost half of what the US spent last year). Medicare for all would increase the US spending by ~50%. 

4.  My opponent also claims that the US has the lowest life expectancy of other developed nations. However, he doesn't account for causation versus correlation. Unfortunately, heart disease, stroke, and diabetes are leading causes of death in America. Those are also medical conditions that have a proven reduced mortality rate with behavioral changes to their health choices.   While our medical system does need to be overhauled to make preventative care more accessible, Medicare for All is not a one-size-fits-all solution.

5.  According to the National Institute of Health, British studies have shown that their National Health Service (a similar version of Medicare for All) doesn’t automatically make everyone healthier. In fact, wealthier individuals were still healthier on average due to them not having sedentary life styles and the ability to use American hospitals.  

Like I've said before, it is important that we can rely on our elected officials to tell us the truth.  I encourage you to read the attached research article from The American Experiment as well as look into their linked articles.  If we're going to fix something, we have to be honest about the real problems and then come up with real, achievable solutions.

Link to article: https://www.americanexperiment.org/candidates-need-a-little-help-on-the-cost-of-medicare-for-all/

Ever wonder how everyday neighbors help shape the direction of our local Republican Party? That’s where Delegates come in.

What do Delegates do?
✔️ Attend BPOU meetings and conventions
✔️ Vote on local party leadership and rules
✔️ Help shape policy priorities and grassroots strategy
✔️ Support candidates and organize locally

Delegates play a critical role in making sure grassroots voices are heard - not just political insiders.

How do you become a delegate?
👉 Attend your precinct caucus on February 3rd
👉 Sign in and participate
👉 Volunteer or be nominated to serve as a delegate
👉 Be elected by your neighbors at caucus
👉 Be elected by your neighbors at the BPOU convention

It’s that simple - and it’s one of the most impactful ways to get involved in your community.

Fiscal Transparency Series — Setting the Record Straight on the FY2026 Continuing Resolution

💬 The Truth About the “Democrat CR”

The Democrats’ six-week “Continuing Resolution” added $10 billion in new short-term spending, plus a permanent $350 billion expansion of the Affordable Care Act.

But here’s the truth:

✅ Only about $1.5–2 billion covers truly immediate needs that keep key programs from lapsing.

❌ The rest is made up of political add-ons, one-time earmarks, or long-term policy changes that don’t belong in a six-week stopgap bill.

⚖️ Where the Money Goes

🔴 Immediate Needs — ~$1.5–2 Billion (Real, Short-Term Necessities)

These items keep vital services running temporarily until the full budget passes:

🍼 WIC Nutrition Program — ~$1.0B
Keeps benefits flowing to mothers and infants. Without it, some state WIC offices could run short by mid-October and cut off new participants.

🏥 Health & Telehealth Program Extensions — ~$0.3–0.5B
Renews funding for rural hospitals, community health centers, and telehealth waivers through Oct. 31. Without this, some programs would lose legal authority.

🎖️ Veterans Housing & Homelessness Programs — ~$0.2–0.3B
Extends VA housing assistance, suicide prevention programs, and HUD veteran housing grants for one month. Prevents temporary service gaps.

➡️ Total: ~$1.5–2 billion (short-term, legitimate needs)

🟩 Can Wait / Add-Ons — ~$8 Billion (Not Urgent)

These items aren’t emergencies — they’re discretionary or political priorities that can wait until the full appropriations process:

🏛️ Corporation for Public Broadcasting — $491 million
Advance payment to PBS/NPR that’s not due until later in FY2026.

🧾 New Inspector General at OMB — $20 million
Creates a new oversight office; useful, but not time-sensitive.

🛡️ Member Security Projects — $156 million
Adds new residential and office security systems for members of Congress; not a program continuation, just an upgrade.

⚖️ Judiciary & Facility Security — $52 million
Funds courthouse security improvements; can safely wait for the full-year budget.

⚙️ Defense & Agency Adjustments — few hundred million combined
Routine technical adjustments for the Navy, NNSA, SBA, and Treasury; both parties already agree on these, no urgency.

➡️ Total: ~$8 billion (short-term extras, not emergencies)

🟦 Permanent Policy Change — $350 Billion Over 10 Years

💊 ACA Subsidy Expansion (Permanent)

Makes the temporary COVID-era ACA premium subsidies permanent — a $350 billion, 10-year cost per the Congressional Budget Office.

That’s long-term mandatory spending being hidden inside a short-term CR.

It doesn’t fix the system — it locks in higher subsidies for insurers while costs keep rising for families.

🩺 The Truth About “Healthcare for Illegal Immigrants”

You’ve probably heard the claim that Democrats “demanded healthcare for illegal immigrants.”
Here’s the real story 👇

❌ No section of the bill provides new benefits to illegal immigrants.

✅ Medicare, Medicaid, and ACA eligibility remain limited to citizens and lawfully present immigrants.

🏥 Community Health Centers have treated everyone for basic or emergency care since the 1970s — that’s old law, not new funding.

🚑 Emergency Medicaid (created under President Reagan in 1986) reimburses hospitals for life-saving emergencies only.

➡️ No new healthcare for illegal immigrants. No change in eligibility. No new money for it.

⚠️ The Bigger Problem: Locking In a Broken System

The ACA subsidy expansion doesn’t fix healthcare — it cements a failing model.

Instead of reforming costs, Democrats want to make temporary subsidies permanent — forcing taxpayers to spend $350 billion more over the next decade without lowering premiums or improving care.

That’s not reform.

That’s budget autopilot — and it’s why Washington’s debt keeps climbing.

🧮 Bottom Line

Democrats’ CR: $10B short-term + $350B long-term spending.

Only ~$2B is truly urgent; the rest are add-ons or permanent expansions.

No new healthcare for illegal immigrants — just recycled political rhetoric.

Republicans passed a Clean CR that keeps the government open without hiding long-term spending inside a six-week bill.

Albany, NY — Ralph Ambrosio, Republican candidate for Congress in New York's 20th Congressional District, is calling for urgent congressional action to confront America's exploding national debt, which he describes as the greatest long-term existential threat to the nation's economic security and a major underlying driver of the affordability crisis facing American families.

"We have a $40 trillion national debt, and Washington is spending more than $1.3 trillion annually just on interest costs. "In my view, this is the greatest existential threat to our nation's economic future and one of the largest underlying drivers of the affordability crisis. Yet the people in Congress responsible for managing our nation's finances continue to avoid having a serious conversation about it. Paul continues to advocate for more taxes, spending, programs, subsidies, and regulations, the very policies that got us into this mess. Ambrosio argues that decades of deficit spending, borrowing, and fiscal mismanagement have contributed to inflationary pressures, higher interest rates, and rising costs for American households and businesses.

"Think about this: when Paul Tonko first went to Washington, our national debt was approximately $10 trillion. Now it is over $40 trillion. "The national debt is not an abstract accounting problem. It is a threat to our prosperity, our national security, and our children's future. Congress needs to stop treating this crisis as somebody else's responsibility. We need leaders who are willing to confront the problem, explain the consequences, and put forward serious solutions. Bill’s no innovator; he's a phoney who profited off others' ideas while stifling real innovation. 

First, consider Steve Jobs. Jobs was a master at blending technology with human intuition. He co-founded Apple in a garage, revolutionized personal computing with the Macintosh's graphical interface, and later saved the company from bankruptcy by unleashing the iPod, iPhone, and iPad. These weren't just products; they were cultural shifts that made technology accessible and beautiful. Jobs anticipated needs we didn't know we had, emphasizing design and user experience over raw specs. Like me at Sticker Mule, where we've custom-built our tech stack to deliver lightning-fast turnarounds, Jobs was hands-on. He demanded perfection, iterating relentlessly on hardware and software. Jobs wasn't about crushing rivals through dirty tricks; he out-innovated them. His vision transformed seven industries, from music to publishing, much like how I've turned a niche printing service into a tech-driven global operation. We're both proof that true technologists create ecosystems that empower people rather than exploit them.

Elon Musk takes that spirit to cosmic levels. Musk built Zip2, sold it for millions, then poured everything into PayPal, revolutionizing online payments. From there, he tackled humanity's grandest challenges: SpaceX with reusable rockets slashing space travel costs, Tesla accelerating the electric vehicle revolution with innovations like the Giga Press, and now Neuralink and xAI pushing AI and brain interfaces. Musk's first-principles thinking—breaking problems down to fundamentals and rebuilding better—is what I apply at Sticker Mule. Every child is different. Sandy and I know that firsthand.

We have four kids who grew up in the same house, with the same parents and the same values, yet each has different strengths, interests, challenges, and ambitions. What helped one thrive wasn’t necessarily what another needed.

That experience shaped how I think about education and why school choice matters. Parents should have the ability to choose an education that fits their child, whether that means a traditional public school, charter school, career and technical program, private education, or another path that works for their family.

Artificial intelligence is already changing the economy, and the jobs our children will compete for ten and twenty years from now will not look exactly like the jobs we know today. We will need people who can work with technology, build things, solve problems, care for others, and bring highly skilled technical expertise to an increasingly advanced economy.

🚨 Data Centers in Chester & Berks Counties: Smart Infrastructure or Speculative Gamble on Power Prices?

After two decades restructuring data centers, I’ve watched the industry reinvent itself every 10–15 years with brutal efficiency — from mainframes in the ‘80s, to colocation in the ‘90s, multi-tenant servers in the 00's, hyperscale clouds in the 10s, and now the AI data center boom.

Each wave doesn’t replace the last because the old tech failed. It gets replaced because the economics and applications change.

That’s exactly why I’m watching the surge of data center proposals in Chester and Berks Counties with deep caution.

These projects aren’t just infrastructure plays. They’re high-stakes bets on two volatile things staying true for decades:

1. Cheap, reliable electricity
2. Low-latency fiber connectivity

Southeastern Pennsylvania looks great on paper. Microsoft’s 20-year deal to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 (targeted for 2027) promises 835 MW of carbon-free baseload power for AI. The major fiber corridor from Boston to D.C. runs right through the region.

But here’s the reality check:

PJM (our regional grid) is already seeing electricity prices climb sharply due to data center-driven demand. Forecasts show data centers could add up to 30 gigawatts of new load by 2030. Capacity auction costs are exploding — billions in extra charges being socialized across all ratepayers. Local utilities like PECO are facing massive interconnection requests that could double peak demand.

Aging transmission lines and substations weren’t built for this kind of always-on, concentrated load. Upgrades cost billions and take years. When developers don’t fully cover them, the cost lands on families and small businesses.

Residents in East Vincent, East Whiteland, and other towns are already pushing back — concerned about grid strain, noise, water use, and the risk that today’s “cheap power” deal becomes tomorrow’s regret.

The fiber advantage is real, but latency-sensitive workloads can (and will) move if power costs rise faster than expected. And they will.

The next industry restructuring cycle is already coming. AI training and inference today could look like yesterday’s commodity servers once the next efficiency breakthrough or location arbitrage appears.

Bottom line: Application still determines everything.

A Wall Street bank can pay premium power prices near New York because microseconds mean billions of dollars. The same rates would kill the economics of AI cat videos or cheap cloud storage.
Unless developers can clearly explain — with real transparency — exactly what high-value workloads will live in these facilities, and why they must be here (not in cheaper-power regions), this isn’t sustainable infrastructure.

It’s real estate speculation on electricity prices and fiber proximity… and our communities could be left holding the bag when the economics shift.

I’m not against data centers done right.

Done right means:

1. Transparent economics
2. Developers paying 100% upfront for grid upgrades
3. Clear, long-term applications that justify the power draw for decades
4. Real answers to tough questions: Who pays if prices double? 5. What happens when the next tech wave hits?

Chester and Berks have a rare opportunity with the TMI restart and the fiber route. Let’s not waste it on speculative projects that treat our grid and communities like a commodity.

Local officials and residents should demand clarity now. The towns that insist on it will thrive in the next restructuring. The ones that don’t may end up with higher electric bills, reliability issues, and regret.

Why is the stock market at all-time highs while consumer confidence is near a 70-year low?

Strangely, a big part of the answer lies in data centers.

I first restructured a data center about 20 years ago — a Silicon Graphics facility that once powered the rendering for films like Toy Story and the first movie of the Jurassic World franchise. Over the past two decades, I’ve restructured others, and what I’m seeing today is unprecedented.

The stock market is hitting record highs largely because of the AI narrative. For these high-valuation companies to justify their multiples, they need two things: rapid growth and continued access to cheap capital. Data center financing is quietly supplying both.

Here’s how it works: Data centers are being funded through three major debt instruments:

1. Loans or leases for the physical real estate
2. Receivables-backed financing from long-term contracts with hyperscalers like Google, Microsoft, and Meta
3. Financing for the AI hardware itself (primarily GPUs from NVIDIA and similar vendors)

This creates an enormous amount of debt financing the AI buildout — much of it largely invisible to traditional stock market analysis. New data centers are sprouting up across the U.S. and around the world, fueled by super-cheap capital, which then drive big-Tech revenues.

And where is this cheap debt coming from? Not primarily from traditional bank loans, but from securitization markets that ultimately feed into money market funds, as well as private credit. If you have money sitting in a money market account, you’re likely helping finance this AI infrastructure. Should things go wrong, there’s an implicit assumption that the Federal Reserve would step in to backstop the paper and stabilize the system — much like it has in past crises.

That’s the mechanical reason behind the market’s strength.

So why is consumer confidence at multi-decade lows?

Because on Main Street, AI feels less like an opportunity and more like a threat. We’re in a global AI arms race, and many people sense what’s coming: potentially massive job displacement. Estimates suggest that 30-40% of tasks in certain fields (like computer programming, legal work, accounting, and creative services) could be automated or fundamentally changed in the coming years.

Young people and recent graduates are desperately trying to “AI-proof” their careers, but those carrying heavy student debt face an especially brutal outlook. Consumers instinctively understand that a painful economic transition may be ahead, with higher structural unemployment possible as entire professions are reshaped. That anxiety is showing up clearly in confidence surveys.

This divergence highlights deeper structural problems: distorted incentives in higher education and student lending, loose monetary policy from the Federal Reserve, and policy choices that have saddled younger generations with debt while making housing, family formation, and entrepreneurship harder than ever.

We’ve built a system that rewards financial engineering and speculative technology investment far more than it supports the real economic security of average citizens. As a result, total U.S. debt (government, corporate, and household) now exceeds $100 trillion — fueling affordability crises in housing, education, and healthcare — while corporations and special interests often face limited downside risk when these speculative and highly leveraged bets falter (part of the reason why we lost 2 hospitals in Chester County for example).

Stocks are partying like it’s 1999, but Americans haven’t been this gloomy in 70 years.

First, I want you to know I am listening. After reading comments and feedback from neighbors on social media from my post on Data Centers, I attended the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission’s (PUC) public hearing yesterday in Malvern on the proposed merger between American Water Works (parent of Pennsylvania American Water) and Essential Utilities (parent of Aqua Pennsylvania).

Residents, business owners, environmental advocates, and local officials spoke with one clear voice: strong opposition. This $40 billion all-stock deal would create an effective monopoly over a resource no one can live without in much of our state.

Key facts on the scale of this merger:

✅ Pennsylvania American Water serves approximately 2.4–2.5 million people across 37–38 counties.
✅ Aqua Pennsylvania serves about 1.5 million people across 32–33 counties.
✅ The combined company would serve 4.7 million water and wastewater connections across 17 states plus military installations — making it the largest private water and wastewater utility in the United States.

Proponents promise “economies of scale.” In reality, this too often means higher profits for shareholders while ratepayers absorb the debt and transaction costs. Consumer filings and protests have already shown that American Water’s rates run substantially higher than Aqua’s in comparable service areas — over 30% higher in some wastewater examples for similar usage.

Pennsylvania is in the midst of a manufacturing resurgence and a massive buildout of data centers. A single hyperscale data center can consume up to 5 million gallons of freshwater per day — roughly the daily water use of a town of 10,000 to 50,000 people. This demand adds enormous pressure to existing residential, agricultural, and industrial needs in a state already facing localized water stresses.

Water is not a discretionary consumer product. It is a public necessity. Consolidating these two giants hands one dominant player control over the pipes, treatment plants, and rates for millions of Pennsylvanians. It reduces options for municipalities and eliminates even the limited competitive pressure that currently exists.

😠How did we get here? More than a century ago, Congress passed the Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) and the Clayton Act (1914) specifically to prevent mergers that “may substantially lessen competition” or “tend to create a monopoly.” Enforcement has weakened over decades under legal standards that favor short-term price effects over long-term structural power — especially dangerous for essential services like water. In short, Congress has not been doing its job for a long time, which over 80% of us know already!

Since Congress isn’t acting, the PUC must step up and prioritize the public interest. Yesterday’s hearing proved that Pennsylvanians are paying attention — and for good reason.

Our water — and the economic future it supports — is too important to become a monopoly profit center. The PUC heard the public. Now it must act.

And until we elect new representatives in Congress who will actually do their job — breaking up the trusts, monopolies, and oligopolies that are making life unaffordable, especially in healthcare (an issue I am deeply passionate about fixing) — state regulators like the PUC are our first and best line of defense.

📢⚡Tell Congress to Stop Funding Bitcoin and Driving Up Our Electric Bills

The next time our PECO or PPL bill shows up higher than expected, remember this: a big chunk of the extra cost comes from cryptocurrency mining and the broader energy surge it drives.

In a conversation I had with former U.S. Bankruptcy Judge David R. Jones — who oversaw several major cryptocurrency bankruptcy cases, including Core Scientific (one of the largest crypto miners) — we both agreed: crypto functions, in practice, not as a currency but as a commodity whose worth is fundamentally based on the cost of the electricity needed to produce it. Judge Jones saw this reality up close while managing the financial wreckage of collapsed mining and crypto lending operations.

₿ Bitcoin isn’t “digital gold.” It is a commodity whose value is directly tied to the massive amounts of electricity required to mine it. Miners only make money if they can sell their Bitcoin for more than it costs to produce — and electricity is by far the biggest cost. As more bitcoins are mined, the network becomes harder to solve, so each new Bitcoin requires more electricity than earlier ones. Early investors understood this dynamic: they were betting that Bitcoin’s price would keep rising as the power needed to mine the next coin grows higher. The more expensive it becomes to produce, the higher the price must go for miners to stay profitable. That’s why Bitcoin now trades in roughly the same range as the current cost to mine it — around $80,000.

Cryptocurrency mining now consumes between 0.6% and 2.3% of all electricity in the United States — roughly the same amount used by entire states like Washington or West Virginia. Because electricity demand is relatively inelastic in the short term, this added load has helped push our power bills up by 5–10% in many PJM areas through higher base rates and capacity charges. 

Here in PA-6, where families already stretch paychecks amid high housing costs and inflation, electricity prices are climbing. Recent rate increases, driven in part by surging demand from cryptocurrency mining operations across PJM, are hitting households hard. Utilities are upgrading infrastructure and securing more capacity, and guess who pays? Not just the miners or tech giants — we do, through higher base rates that don’t care whether we own crypto or not. In other words, when we look at our next PECO or PPL bill, 5–10% of it could be going to support cryptocurrency mining.

Beyond higher bills, the environmental toll is severe. Crypto mining’s explosive electricity demand is keeping older coal-fired plants running longer and increasing carbon emissions across the PJM region, where new load is often met by coal and natural gas. In PJM, this creates “carbon leakage”: demand from crypto operations pulls more coal-generated power from Pennsylvania, Ohio, and West Virginia, raising local emissions and worsening air quality for Chester and Berks County families.

Right here in Pennsylvania, operations like the Scrubgrass and Panther Creek waste-coal plants have ramped up burning specifically to feed crypto mining, spiking sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and CO₂ output. Globally, Bitcoin mining alone has been equivalent to burning tens of billions of pounds of coal in emissions impact. This isn’t clean innovation — it’s dirty externalities that all Pennsylvanians breathe and pay for.

The late Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett’s longtime partner and one of the clearest thinkers in American business, cut through the hype years ago. He called Bitcoin “stupid,” “evil,” and something that makes its promoters look bad in comparison to honest work. Munger warned that it undermines sound money and creates massive externalities. He was right. We’re all subsidizing a speculative asset that delivers no goods, no services, and no productivity — just higher bills and dirtier air for the rest of us.

Blockchain technology has legitimate uses: secure supply chains, fraud-resistant records, efficient contracting in specific industries. Those applications deserve support. But proof-of-work crypto mining — the dominant model for Bitcoin — is different. It turns kilowatt-hours into lottery tickets, and Pennsylvania ratepayers and taxpayers are footing part of the tab while the grid strains and emissions rise.

Now comes the latest proposal in Washington: the BITCOIN Act, introduced by Senator Cynthia Lummis and Representative Nick Begich. This legislation directs the Treasury to purchase 1 million Bitcoins over the next five years — 200,000 BTC per year — and hold them for at least 20 years. At current prices, that’s a government commitment of roughly $80 billion in new purchases on top of the hundreds of thousands of BTC already held from forfeitures.

The bill claims this spending is “budget-neutral,” but the mechanism is clear: it diverts the first $6 billion per year in Federal Reserve remittances — money that currently helps reduce the federal deficit or fund general government operations — straight into buying Bitcoin. In plain terms, Washington wants to redirect tens of billions of taxpayer-backed dollars to stockpile a volatile digital commodity whose rising price is fueled by the very electricity demand driving up our utility costs here in Pennsylvania.

Pennsylvanians are practical people. We want real innovation, reliable and affordable energy, and a government that doesn’t pick winners with our money. Crypto mining fails that test. It raises costs for families, manufacturers, and small businesses across Chester and Berks Counties while delivering concentrated gains to a narrow group of speculators — all while adding to our environmental burden.

We should welcome genuine technological progress — including efficient blockchain uses that don’t torch the grid or the atmosphere. But we must stop forcing every Pennsylvania household to subsidize Bitcoin’s appetite. Our grid, our air, and our tax dollars belong to all of us, not to the loudest promoters of digital gold. It’s time for policies that protect ratepayers, the environment, and fiscal responsibility first.

That’s why I’m running for Congress in PA-6. Families in West Chester, Downingtown, Reading, and across Chester and Berks Counties deserve a Representative who will fight to protect our wallets, our grid, and our air — not someone who rubber-stamps Washington schemes that drive up our electric bills and dirty our communities. We need practical leadership that puts Pennsylvania ratepayers and working families first: affordable and reliable energy, real fiscal responsibility, and innovation that doesn’t force us to subsidize speculative gains. I’m running to bring common sense back to Congress so our tax dollars and electric bills work for us — not for Bitcoin miners and their allies in Washington.

What West Point Taught Me About the Stakes with Iran

As a physics major at West Point — West Point - The U.S. Military Academy — I studied the science and effects of nuclear weapons — not to build them, but to understand how to deter and defend against them. We used the declassified reference The Effects of Nuclear Weapons and ran calculations on yields, blast effects, and potential consequences (see posted photo of my OG Army-issued Nuclear Bomb Effects Computer from West Point). That taxpayer-funded education was designed to prepare officers for one of the gravest responsibilities an American leader can face.

Today, those same lessons feel urgently relevant.

Recent reports and disclosures from Iranian negotiators indicate Iran has amassed roughly 460 kilograms of uranium enriched to 60% — material that could be quickly processed into fuel for multiple nuclear weapons. With their existing ballistic missiles and drone technology, the timeline to a deliverable threat has shortened dramatically. Through the Manhattan Project we were able to build nuclear bombs in a few short years with 1940s technology (like the Analog Computer in the attached photo).

The human and economic costs of even one such weapon used against a city would be devastating: massive loss of life, destroyed infrastructure, and long-term health and environmental consequences. These are sobering realities, not hypotheticals.

At the same time, Americans are rightly weary of prolonged military engagements. Many of us — veterans, families, and taxpayers — have paid a heavy price for conflicts without clear endpoints or sufficient congressional oversight.

That is why the War Powers Resolution of 1973 matters. Passed after Vietnam to restore Congress’s constitutional role, it requires the President to notify Congress and limits unauthorized military action to 60 days (with a possible 30-day extension). That deadline arrives on May 1st. Unless Congress declares war or passes a specific Authorization for Use of Military Force, U.S. forces must begin to withdraw.

This moment gives us an opportunity for deliberate, bipartisan decision-making. I respect that Chrissy Houlahan — a fellow veteran serving on the House Armed Services Committee — has strongly argued for Congress to exercise its constitutional authority under the War Powers Resolution and to avoid another open-ended conflict without clear strategy or oversight. She and I agree that the American people deserve a voice through their elected representatives.

As someone who served as both an Army officer and chaplain — counseling service members and families through the real costs of war — I believe we must weigh two vital priorities:

✅Preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons, which would destabilize the entire region and threaten American interests.

✅Avoiding another open-ended conflict that drains our resources and risks American lives without a clear strategy.

The education I received at West Point, paid for by American taxpayers, should help all of us have an informed conversation — not just in Washington, but here in Chester and Berks counties.

The fundamental question before our nation is this: Should the United States allow Iran to become a nuclear power?

If the answer is no — as I believe it must be — then the President and Congress need to work together on a clear, limited strategy with measurable goals and regular oversight. If the answer is yes, then we should de-escalate and prepare to deter a nuclear Iran through other means.

Either path requires honest debate and congressional approval. Our system of checks and balances exists for exactly these moments.

What do you think? I welcome your thoughts as we consider the best path forward for our country, our troops, and our communities. And, I urge you to share your thoughts with my opponent and our current U.S. Representative Chrissy Houlahan..

🏠 Re-Privatizing Fannie and Freddie: Don’t Introduce New Risks — Fix Housing Affordability First

Bill Ackman’s push to re-privatize Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac — releasing them from conservatorship, restructuring or forgiving Treasury’s senior preferred stock, easing capital rules, and handing greater control to private shareholders — sounds like reform. It is not. In the current environment, it would privatize gains while leaving taxpayers with the downside, all without fixing what is driving the housing crisis.

Fannie and Freddie play a vital role as government-sponsored enterprises. They buy conforming loans (up to the current baseline limit of $832,750 in areas like Berks and Chester Counties in Pennsylvania), securitize them into mortgage-backed securities, and guarantee timely payment of principal and interest. This government-backed assurance, backed by real estate collateral, provides essential liquidity and keeps U.S. mortgage rates lower and more stable than a purely private market would deliver.

Since the 2008 bailout of roughly $191 billion, the GSEs have remitted well over $300 billion to taxpayers through dividends, sweeps, and guarantee fees (currently around 65 basis points). The system has been a net revenue generator while delivering systemic stability.

❌ The Real Source of the Housing Crisis

After spending time talking with real estate agents, home builders, and local housing professionals here in Chester County, one thing is clear: America’s housing affordability crisis is the direct result of two intersecting policy failures.

First, high conforming loan limits now support government-backed financing for homes approaching or exceeding $1 million. Second, excessive regulatory costs — zoning restrictions, lengthy permitting, environmental mandates, impact fees, and construction requirements — make it far more profitable for builders to focus on these larger, high-end homes instead of smaller, affordable starter or retirement units.

This combination severely distorts the market. New home construction has lagged long-term demand, remaining well below the levels needed to keep pace with population growth and household formation. As a direct consequence, most people in their twenties and thirties are effectively squeezed out of homeownership altogether. This is why first-time buyers now average around 40 years old in Pennsylvania.

💰 Leave the GSEs Alone — Fix Affordability First
Rather than rushing re-privatization and introducing new risks into an already unbalanced system that heavily favors million-dollar homes, we should leave Fannie and Freddie in their current conservatorship structure. The existing hybrid model provides proven liquidity and taxpayer returns. Changing it now would risk higher borrowing costs or weaker safeguards without addressing root causes.

🏠  Instead, policymakers should focus aggressively on the affordability crisis:

✅ Targeted lower rates for starter homes: The Federal Reserve should implement policies that deliver meaningfully lower interest rates specifically for smaller, entry-level homes (for example, those priced at or below the local median). This would help rebalance incentives away from luxury properties and make homeownership more accessible for younger families.

In fact, I have argued that 0% rate, fee-only loans up to the median home price (about $400K) that amortize over 10-15 years is what is needed to fix the market. The Federal Reserve could do this without new government consent to better achieve its dual mandates of low inflation and high employment, but Congress should be proactive in this regard. We should remember that the Federal Reserve provided near-zero rates for a long time, but the main beneficiaries were asset managers and wealthy investors — not average American families — since it was untargeted. But if the Federal Reserve targeted support for homes below median cost, it would be transformative and beneficial not just for young people but also for older folks and retirees. In other words, the Federal Reserve needs to use the same 0% QE tool it has in the past, but just in a targeted way.

✅ Attack regulatory barriers head-on: Slash zoning restrictions, streamline permitting, reduce unnecessary mandates, and lower construction-related costs at the local, state, and federal levels. These changes would encourage builders to construct the smaller starter and retirement homes that families actually need, increasing overall supply where it matters most.

Housing finance is inherently cyclical. Maintaining the current GSE backstop as a public good prevents localized problems from becoming national crises. But we cannot keep subsidizing million-dollar homes with taxpayer-backed guarantees while regulatory barriers block affordable construction for everyone else. Fix the supply distortions and rate misalignments first.

Only then will the system truly serve American families rather than high-end developers and investors. The housing market and younger Americans deserve solutions that expand opportunity, not experiments that shift more risk onto taxpayers. Keeping Fannie and Freddie stable while directly tackling regulatory barriers and delivering lower rates for starter homes is the practical way forward.

The sudden loss of two cherished Henderson High School graduates has left a profound void in our Chester County community. Corporal Timothy J. O'Connor Jr., a 40-year-old Pennsylvania State Police trooper with 15 years of dedicated service, and Megan K. Nieberle, a 53-year-old CHOP nurse who cared for children for 27 years, were taken far too soon in separate tragedies just one day apart in March 2026.

Tim embodied selfless service from his youth—leadership, compassion, and a commitment to protecting others, seen in his firefighting days and throughout his State Police career. A devoted husband to Casey, father to young Kenzie, son, brother, and friend, his warmth touched countless lives. He stepped into uncertainty daily to keep us safe, leaving a legacy of courage that inspires us still.

Megan was the heart of her family and community—a mother of three, wife, sister, and daughter fiercely loved for her warmth, humor, loyalty, and compassion. At Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, she touched countless patients, families, and colleagues as a skilled nurse and leader in surgical services. Her death in a random act of violence shattered those who knew her, yet it sparked an outpouring of support, including fundraisers to help her family heal.

Rooted in the same high school halls, their lives remind us of our deep interconnectedness. Tim fell in the line of duty during a routine traffic stop; Megan in a senseless shooting. In Megan's case, the heartbreak deepens: hours earlier, Tredyffrin Township police encountered the suspect exhibiting erratic, paranoid behavior and openly armed. They escorted him for a voluntary mental health evaluation, but he refused treatment and left—prompting painful community questions about prevention. Investigations continue, highlighting the immense complexity of such moments.

These tragedies underscore a hard truth: law enforcement work is extraordinarily demanding. Officers confront danger daily, making split-second decisions under pressure, navigating mental health crises, legal constraints, gun laws, and incomplete information—often in chaotic situations where hindsight reveals tough realities. They are human beings striving to do their best.

As an Army chaplain called to nurture the living, care for the wounded, and honor the dead, I see these losses as a call to extend that sacred mission into our civilian lives.

We nurture the living by supporting officers and their families with spiritual guidance, counseling, and resources to build resilience amid heavy burdens. We care for the wounded—not just the physically injured, but families carrying invisible scars of worry and fear, and officers processing tragic outcomes—through empathy, mental health support, family programs, and simple kindness. We honor the dead by keeping Tim's sacrifice and Megan's healing legacy alive in memorials, tributes, and honest reflection on better equipping first responders for crises.

In the words of Casey O’Connor at her husband's funeral: “Please continue the good work that you do every single day. Do not let the bad of the world tarnish your mission of protecting with integrity.”

Let us heed her plea. We must advocate for enhanced training, mental health resources, and protocols for crisis intervention; strengthen community bonds to ease family strains; and offer prayers, presence, and support so no one feels alone.

In nurturing the living, caring for the wounded, and honoring the dead, we ensure no sacrifice is forgotten and no family unsupported. May Tim and Megan's memories inspire us to greater compassion, gratitude for those who protect us, and renewed commitment to stand with law enforcement officers and the families who stand with them every day. I will remember both of them every time I pass Henderson High School. 

With gratitude for their service and lives, and solidarity with all who mourn. 💙

The government just passed a law to automatically register 100% of young American men aged 18–25 for Selective Service by December 2026. Yet less than 30% of young American men are medically qualified to serve — the rest are disqualified mostly due to medical conditions, weight issues, and mental health problems.

Why? Over half of American kids are on Medicaid/CHIP, trapped in a broken healthcare system plagued by fraud, waste, abuse, and inefficiency that too often fails to deliver quality care.

Here’s the common-sense fix: If Washington can mass-enroll every 18-year-old man for the draft registry, it can mass-enroll all American kids into the Young Americans Healthcare Plan.
This plan leverages the proven TRICARE model — which already successfully covers nearly 10 million Americans at a fraction of the cost of Medicaid/CHIP and private insurance. TRICARE was designed to keep military members and their families deployment-ready. Our children deserve that same high-quality care.

This would dramatically increase the number of young people who are medically fit to serve, solve a huge chunk of healthcare affordability, slash taxpayer waste, and save families at least $5,000 a year — while building a healthier, stronger next generation.

Priorities matter.

In the mid-1990s, we were involved in intense special operations on the submarine I was serving on as the boat's Assistant Navigator. 

We were initially cleared to enter port for a quick port call, supply load, etc. We were exhausted, struggling to do what was necessary. At the last minute, the country rescinded authorization to tie up to a pier. 

The best Commanding Officer I ever had the privilege to serve under, Captain Brad McDonald, said: “screw this”. He decided to anchor in the Harbor. Trust me when I say you never use the anchor on a submarine. He did it. 

He then sent our SEAL/EOD team into port (we had rigid inflatables on board) with a bunch of money the wardroom collected (think officers). Every dollar was spent on beer. CAPT Brad allowed a rotation topside so every Sailor could have a beer. 

Nothing soft or entitled on this crew. The best band of pirates I ever deployed with. We went on to conduct operations never done before in the great history of submarines.

Two days, one beer, a refreshed, tough-as-nails CREW, ready to get back in the fight. Even the best of the best perform better when they get rest, distraction, life. Strong leaders understand that; the weak ones do not. Thank you, Captain McDonald for being the strongest of the strong.

A BILL 

To improve access to evidence-based mental health services, strengthen family and community resilience, support veterans and first responders, address root causes of mental health challenges, and promote faith-based and local solutions, without creating new expansive federal bureaucracies or unfunded mandates.

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled,

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE; TABLE OF CONTENTS.

(a) Short Title.  This Act may be cited as the “Mental Health Access and Family Resilience Act” or “MHARA.”

(b) Table of Contents. 

Sec. 1. Short title; table of contents.
Sec. 2. Findings and purpose.
Sec. 3. Definitions.
Sec. 4. Expanding access to mental health services.
Sec. 5. Veterans and first responders’ mental health support.
Sec. 6. Family resilience and prevention.
Sec. 7. Workforce development and provider training.
Sec. 8. Suicide prevention and crisis intervention.
Sec. 9. Integration with substance abuse prevention and treatment.
Sec. 10. Addressing homelessness as a mental health and family stability priority.
Sec. 11. Youth and school-based family partnerships.
Sec. 12. Research, innovation, and data collection.
Sec. 13. Accountability, oversight, and reporting.
Sec. 14. Authorization of appropriations.
Sec. 15. Effective date; sunset provision.

SECTION 2. FINDINGS AND PURPOSE.

Congress finds the following:

(1) Strong families, faith communities, and personal responsibility form the foundation of mental resilience, as evidenced by reduced rates of depression, substance abuse, and suicide in stable family structures.

(2) Veterans, first responders, and residents in underserved communities, including Bexar County and Texas’s 20th Congressional District, face disproportionate mental health challenges, including PTSD, trauma from service, and economic stressors.

(3) Root causes such as family breakdown, substance abuse, gang violence, and limited community-based support must be addressed alongside clinical services.

(4) Expanding access to telehealth, peer support, and faith-informed counseling, while incentivizing private and local innovation, provides cost-effective, dignity-affirming care.

(5) Substance use disorders and mental health conditions frequently co-occur, exacerbating cycles of family breakdown, unemployment, and instability, particularly among veterans and in high-poverty areas like parts of Bexar County.

(6) Homelessness is often intertwined with untreated mental illness and substance abuse; stable housing paired with voluntary, family-centered treatment and personal accountability promotes long-term recovery and resilience.

The purpose of this Act is to enhance mental health access, build family resilience, and empower communities and veterans through targeted, accountable measures.

SECTION 3. DEFINITIONS.

(1) Family Resilience Programs: Evidence-based initiatives that strengthen marriage, parenting, and intergenerational support networks.

(2) Faith-Based Providers: Nonprofit organizations operating consistently with sincerely held religious beliefs that deliver mental health support.

(3) Veterans: Individuals who served in the uniformed services, as defined in section 101 of title 38, United States Code.

(4) Telehealth: Includes audio-visual and audio-only services compliant with HIPAA.

SECTION 4. EXPANDING ACCESS TO MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES.

(a) Medicaid and CHIP Flexibility. States may use Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program funds for intensive community-based mental health services, including peer support and family counseling, with emphasis on veterans and children.

(b) Telehealth Expansion. The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall extend and simplify telehealth coverage for mental health services in rural and underserved areas, including Texas districts, with parity for audio-only when clinically appropriate.

(c) Block Grants for Community Providers. Authorizes $20 million annually (subject to appropriations) in competitive grants to States and localities for community mental health clinics, prioritizing partnerships with veterans’ organizations, faith-based groups, and family-focused nonprofits.

SECTION 5. VETERANS AND FIRST RESPONDERS’ MENTAL HEALTH SUPPORT.

(a) VA Peer Support Enhancement. Directs the Department of Veterans Affairs to expand peer-to-peer counseling programs, including the “Be There” program and veteran-serving organizations.

(b) Caregiver Support. Provides grants for caregiver mental health training and respite services for families of veterans with service-connected conditions.

(c) Law Enforcement and First Responders. Authorizes grants for officer wellness, peer support, and stigma-reduction programs modeled on successful bipartisan initiatives.

SECTION 6. FAMILY RESILIENCE AND PREVENTION.

(a) Family Strengthening Grants. Establishes a grant program through the Department of Health and Human Services for evidence-based programs that promote marriage education, parenting skills, and family counseling, with priority for high-poverty areas like parts of San Antonio.

(b) School-Based Family Partnerships. Encourages (without mandates) local educational agencies to partner with community organizations for voluntary family resilience workshops.

(c) Root Cause Initiatives. Supports data-driven programs addressing substance abuse, gang intervention, and fatherhood initiatives as preventive mental health measures.

SECTION 7. WORKFORCE DEVELOPMENT AND PROVIDER TRAINING.

(a) Mental Health Workforce Grants. The Secretary of Health and Human Services shall establish a competitive grant program to States and eligible entities (including community colleges, veterans’ organizations, and faith-based institutions) to recruit, train, and retain mental health professionals, with priority for providers serving rural and underserved areas, veterans, and families.

(b) Training Emphasis. Grants shall support evidence-based training in trauma-informed care, family systems approaches, peer support, and integration of faith-based counseling where appropriate and consistent with provider's mission.

(c) Loan Repayment Incentives. Authorizes expansion of existing loan repayment programs for mental health providers committing to service in high-need districts, including Bexar County, Texas.

SECTION 8. SUICIDE PREVENTION AND CRISIS INTERVENTION.

(a) 988 Lifeline Enhancement. Directs the Secretary to strengthen the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline with improved routing to local, community, and faith-based responders.

(b) Veterans Suicide Prevention. Expands VA programs modeled on successful peer and community initiatives, including outreach to veterans’ families.

(c) Community Crisis Response. Authorizes grants for local crisis stabilization units and mobile response teams that prioritize de-escalation, family involvement, and diversion from hospitalization or incarceration.

SECTION 9. INTEGRATION WITH SUBSTANCE ABUSE PREVENTION AND TREATMENT.

(a) Co-Occurring Disorders Coordination. The Secretary of Health and Human Services, in coordination with the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, shall improve integration of mental health and substance use disorder services through joint funding opportunities, shared screening protocols, and care coordination models that prioritize evidence-based treatment for co-occurring conditions.

(b) Prevention and Early Intervention. Authorizes grants to States and localities for community-based programs targeting root causes, including opioid misuse, methamphetamine, fentanyl, and alcohol abuse, with emphasis on veteran-specific outreach, family involvement, peer recovery coaches, and faith-based recovery support networks.

(c) Treatment and Recovery Expansion. Supports expansion of residential and outpatient treatment programs, including family-centered recovery options and incentives for long-term sobriety through job training and mentorship tied to personal responsibility.

(d) Veterans Focus. Directs the VA to enhance programs addressing substance use alongside PTSD and other service-related conditions, building on successful peer support and community reintegration models.

(e) Accountability Measures. Programs funded under this section shall emphasize measurable outcomes such as reduced relapse rates, family reunification, and decreased justice system involvement, with preference for providers demonstrating cost-effectiveness and voluntary participation.

SECTION 10. ADDRESSING HOMELESSNESS AS A MENTAL HEALTH AND FAMILY STABILITY PRIORITY.

(a) Housing-First with Treatment Integration. Authorizes competitive grants to local governments, veterans’ organizations, faith-based nonprofits, and community providers for supportive housing programs that combine stable housing with voluntary mental health and substance abuse treatment, prioritizing veterans, families, and individuals with co-occurring disorders.

(b) Local Innovation and Accountability. Grants shall favor evidence-based approaches that encourage personal responsibility, family reunification where appropriate, and partnerships with job training and life-skills programs. Nothing in this section shall mandate Housing First models that de-emphasize treatment or enable ongoing substance abuse.

(c) Veterans and Family Emphasis. Expands eligibility and funding flexibility for VA and HUD programs serving homeless veterans with mental health needs, including caregiver support and transitional housing that strengthens family units. Prioritizes projects in high-need districts such as TX-20.

(d) Crisis Diversion and Prevention. Supports mobile outreach teams, crisis stabilization centers, and rapid rehousing initiatives that divert individuals from streets or emergency rooms into treatment and housing pathways, with strong coordination between mental health providers, law enforcement, and community organizations.

(e) Reporting and Safeguards. Recipients must report on outcomes including housing stability, treatment engagement, reduced recidivism to homelessness, and cost savings. Protects religious liberty for faith-based providers and prohibits the use of funds to promote or enable illegal drug use.

SECTION 11. YOUTH AND SCHOOL-BASED FAMILY PARTNERSHIPS.

(a) Voluntary Programs. Encourages local educational agencies to partner with families and community organizations for voluntary mental health education, resilience-building, and parental involvement workshops.

(b) Child and Adolescent Focus. Authorizes targeted grants for early intervention services emphasizing family stability, avoiding ideological approaches, and protecting parental rights.

(c) No Mandates. Nothing in this section shall be construed to impose new requirements on schools or infringe on local control or parental authority.

SECTION 12. RESEARCH, INNOVATION, AND DATA COLLECTION.

(a) Evidence-Based Research. Directs the National Institutes of Health, in coordination with the Department of Veterans Affairs, to prioritize research on family resilience factors, faith-informed interventions, and cost-effective community models.

(b) Outcome Metrics. Requires standardized data collection on program effectiveness, focusing on reduced suicide rates, hospitalizations, substance use, and improved family stability indicators.

(c) Innovation Grants. Establishes limited demonstration projects for novel local solutions, with rigorous evaluation and sunset after 3 years.

SECTION 13. ACCOUNTABILITY, OVERSIGHT, AND REPORTING.

(a) Reporting Requirements. The Secretary of HHS and the Secretary of VA shall submit annual reports to Congress on outcomes, including metrics on reduced hospitalizations, suicide rates, and family stability indicators.

(b) Sunset Provision. This Act shall expire after 5 years unless reauthorized, ensuring fiscal responsibility.

(c) No New Entitlements. Nothing in this Act shall be construed to create an individual entitlement to services.

SECTION 14. AUTHORIZATION OF APPROPRIATIONS.

There are authorized to be appropriated such sums as may be necessary to carry out this Act for fiscal years 2027 through 2031, with amounts allocated across sections subject to annual appropriations and oversight to ensure fiscal responsibility.

SECTION 15. EFFECTIVE DATE; SUNSET PROVISION.

(a) This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.
